sections.title: Section 1: Diving into AI First Java Programming

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Your First Java Program
chapters.goal: Build a simple application using an IDE and AI tooling and learn the syntax of Java that makes your program run.

examples.title: Hello World
examples.description: Write a simple Hello World program in Java.
examples.prompt: Write a Hello World program in Java.

explanation.summary: This is the traditional first Java program: it prints the single line "Hello, World!" to the screen and then ends. Everything else in the file is the minimum structure Java requires before you are allowed to run one statement.

lines.text: Every Java statement lives inside a class, and the class name must match the file name exactly, so this code has to be saved as HelloWorld.java. Getting this pair out of step is the most common first error a beginner meets.

This is the entry point: when you run the program, Java looks for a method with precisely this signature and starts there. The words are not decoration, and changing any of them means Java can no longer find where to begin.

System.out is the standard output stream (your console) and println writes the text followed by a newline. The text in double quotes is a string literal, printed exactly as typed, and the semicolon ends the statement.

Braces come in pairs and close in the reverse order they were opened: this last one closes the class, after the inner braces have closed main. Indentation is only for human readers, but keeping it tidy is how you spot a missing brace.

replay.prompt: Write a Hello World program in Java.
commentary: This is the traditional first Java program: it prints the single line "Hello, World!" to the screen and then ends. Everything else in the file is the minimum structure Java requires before you are allowed to run one statement.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Dynamic Programming with Variables and Input
chapters.goal: Generate an application that you can interact with and learn how variables act as the memory of software programs.

examples.title: Variable Declaration
examples.description: Declare variables in Java to remember values for later.
examples.prompt: Create a reminder by declaring a String variable and print the reminder.
response: String reminder = "Don't forget to submit the report by 5 PM.";

explanation.summary: This program stores a reminder message in a variable and then prints that variable to the console. It is the first step beyond printing text directly: the text now lives in a named container that can be reused and changed in one place.

lines.text: The class name must match the file name exactly, so this code belongs in a file called DisplayReminder.java.

lines.code: String reminder = "Don't forget to submit the report by 5 PM.";
lines.text: Java requires you to state the type of data a variable holds, so the declaration begins with String, the type used for text. The name reminder is the label you use to refer to that text later, and the value in double quotes is what gets stored in it.
Notice there are no quotation marks here: passing reminder without quotes tells Java to look up the value stored in the variable, whereas "reminder" would print the word itself.

replay.prompt: Create a reminder by declaring a String variable and print the reminder.
commentary: This program stores a reminder message in a variable and then prints that variable to the console. It is the first step beyond printing text directly: the text now lives in a named container that can be reused and changed in one place.

examples.title: Print Number
examples.description: Create a Java program that displays a number variable.

prompts.prompt: Write code that prints a number variable.

explanation.summary: This program stores the number 42 in a variable and prints it to the console. It is the same shape as the reminder example, but the variable holds a number instead of text.

lines.text: The type comes first: `int` tells Java this variable holds a whole number, so the value 42 is stored as a number rather than as text. Try changing 42 to your own favorite number and running the program again.
There are no quotation marks around `number`, so Java prints the value stored in the variable rather than the word "number". Wrapping it in quotes is the most common beginner slip here.

replay.prompt: Write code that prints a number variable.
commentary: This program stores the number 42 in a variable and prints it to the console. It is the same shape as the reminder example, but the variable holds a number instead of text.

prompts.prompt: Update the code to add two numbers and display their sum.

explanation.summary: This program stores two whole numbers in variables, adds them together into a third variable, and prints the result. It is the previous PrintNumber example extended to perform a mathematical operation.

lines.text: A variable declaration names a piece of memory and gives it a value; `int` means it holds a whole number, so `a` can be used later anywhere the value 20 would work.

The AI might have picked different numbers, or added them directly inside `println` and skipped the `sum` variable entirely. Variations like these are fine as long as the code is clear and the result is the same.
The `+` operator adds the two values, and the result is stored in a new variable named `sum`. Naming the result makes the intent of the calculation obvious to anyone reading the code.
Passing the variable rather than a number prints whatever `sum` currently holds, so changing the values of `a` and `b` changes the output without touching this line.

replay.prompt: Update the code to add two numbers and display their sum.
commentary: This program stores two whole numbers in variables, adds them together into a third variable, and prints the result. It is the previous PrintNumber example extended to perform a mathematical operation.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Short and Int
examples.description: Explore the differences between short and int data types in Java.
examples.prompt: Write intro code using both a short data type and an int data type.
response: int sum = shortValue + intValue;    // short promoted to int
short doubled = (short) (shortValue * 2); // cast back to short

explanation.summary: This program stores one whole number in a short variable and a larger one in an int, then shows what happens when the two are used together in arithmetic. It prints both values along with their sum and the doubled short.

lines.text: A short reserves only 16 bits, so it holds whole numbers from -32,768 to 32,767 — enough for 12,345 but nowhere near a million. The underscores in the literal are purely for readability; Java ignores them, so 12_345 and 12345 are the same number.
An int uses 32 bits and comfortably holds a million, which is why it is the everyday choice for whole numbers when memory is not tight.

lines.code: int sum = shortValue + intValue;    // short promoted to int
lines.text: Java automatically widens the short to an int before adding, because moving to a larger type cannot lose any part of the value. This is implicit widening casting, and you never have to ask for it.

lines.code: short doubled = (short) (shortValue * 2); // cast back to short
lines.text: Multiplying a short produces an int result, so storing it back into a short is a narrowing conversion that Java refuses to do on its own. The (short) in front is you taking responsibility for the fit — and since 24,690 is under 32,767, nothing is lost here.
The + between a string and a number is concatenation, not addition: Java converts shortValue to text and joins it onto the label.

replay.prompt: Write intro code using both a short data type and an int data type.
commentary: This program stores one whole number in a short variable and a larger one in an int, then shows what happens when the two are used together in arithmetic. It prints both values along with their sum and the doubled short.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Widening Type Casting
examples.description: Explore widening type casting in Java by converting integer variables to double in a calculation.
examples.prompt: Write code to calculate splitting the length of a piece of printer paper into 2 pieces, converting two integer variables to a double in the calculation.
response: int paperLengthInches = 11; // length of printer paper (US Letter long side)

explanation.summary: This program divides an 11-inch sheet of printer paper into 2 equal pieces and prints the length of each piece. Because the two measurements are stored as whole numbers, they are widened to double so the division keeps its fractional part.

lines.code: int paperLengthInches = 11; // length of printer paper (US Letter long side)
lines.text: The paper's length is a whole number of inches, so int is the natural type to hold it. The comment records where the value came from, which is exactly what comments are for.

The (double) in front of each value is the widening cast: it promotes each int to a decimal type before the division happens, so the result is 5.5 rather than 5. Without the casts Java would divide integer by integer, throw away the remainder, and quietly give the wrong answer.
The + here joins text to a number: Java converts eachPieceLength to its printable form and glues the three parts into one line of output.

replay.prompt: Write code to calculate splitting the length of a piece of printer paper into 2 pieces, converting two integer variables to a double in the calculation.
commentary: This program divides an 11-inch sheet of printer paper into 2 equal pieces and prints the length of each piece. Because the two measurements are stored as whole numbers, they are widened to double so the division keeps its fractional part.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Narrow Type Casting
examples.description: Explore narrowing type casting in Java by converting a double variable to an int.
examples.prompt: Write code to narrow casting by displaying an integer value of a price of $100.30 for an advertisement.
response: int adPrice = (int) price; // narrow casting from double to int

explanation.summary: This program stores a price with cents in a double and then converts it to an int, dropping the decimal part so an advertisement can show a round dollar amount. It prints $100 instead of $100.30.

lines.text: The real selling price needs a type that holds decimals, so it goes in a double.

lines.code: int adPrice = (int) price; // narrow casting from double to int
lines.text: The (int) written in front of price is an explicit cast: because an int cannot hold decimals, Java requires you to state the target type as a way of confirming you accept the loss.

lines.code: int adPrice = (int) price; // narrow casting from double to int
lines.text: Narrowing truncates rather than rounds, so 100.30 becomes 100 — and 100.99 would also become 100, not 101.
Joining the number to a string with + turns it into text for display, which is why the dollar sign can sit right next to the value.

replay.prompt: Write code to narrow casting by displaying an integer value of a price of $100.30 for an advertisement.
commentary: This program stores a price with cents in a double and then converts it to an int, dropping the decimal part so an advertisement can show a round dollar amount. It prints $100 instead of $100.30.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Float and Double
examples.description: Explore the differences between float and double data types in Java.
examples.prompt: Write intro code using both a float data type and a double data type.
response: double sum = f + d;              // float promoted to double
float narrowed = (float) d;      // explicit cast from double to float

explanation.summary: This program stores the value of pi in two decimal types \  64-bit double, prints both, then adds them and converts the double back down to a float. It shows how Java handles decimal numbers of different sizes and what happens when you squeeze the larger one into the smaller one.

lines.text: The trailing f is required: Java treats every decimal literal as a double by default, so without it the compiler refuses to put 3.14 into a float variable.
A double has room for roughly twice as many significant digits, which is why it is the usual choice for calculations where precision loss matters.

lines.code: double sum = f + d;              // float promoted to double
lines.text: When a float and a double are added, Java widens the float to a double automatically and the result is a double \ no cast needed, because nothing can be lost going up in size.

lines.code: float narrowed = (float) d;      // explicit cast from double to float
lines.text: Going the other direction discards digits, so Java makes you write the cast to confirm you accept the loss.
Compare this line's output with the printed double: the tail of pi is simply gone, which is narrowing precision loss you can see.

replay.prompt: Write intro code using both a float data type and a double data type.
commentary: This program stores the value of pi in two decimal types \  64-bit double, prints both, then adds them and converts the double back down to a float. It shows how Java handles decimal numbers of different sizes and what happens when you squeeze the larger one into the smaller one.

examples.title: Java Data Types: Boolean
examples.description: Explore the boolean data type in Java.
examples.prompt: Write intro code using a boolean data type without using logic like an if statement.
response: // Combine booleans with logical operators (no if/switch/?:)

explanation.summary: This program shows Java's boolean type, which holds only true or false. It creates booleans directly, derives them from number comparisons, and combines them with logical operators, printing each result.

lines.text: A boolean variable has exactly two possible values, true and false, written as bare keywords with no quotation marks.

A comparison is itself an expression that produces a boolean, so the result of == can be stored in a variable rather than tested immediately. Note that == compares values while a single = assigns, which is a common slip.
The ! operator flips a boolean to its opposite and && produces true only when both sides are true, so this variable means that not everything passed but something did.
Several conditions can be chained with && to form a single yes-or-no answer; because allPassed is false here, readyToSubmit is false no matter what the other two say.
Joining a boolean to a string with + converts it automatically to the text true or false, which is how the program reports its results without any if statement.

examples.title: Pizza Party Calculator
examples.description: Create a pizza calculator in Java that calculates the number of pizzas needed based on the number of people in a party and slices per pizza.
examples.prompt: Write a simple pizza calculator with variables for people in party and slices per pizza.

explanation.summary: This program figures out how many pizzas to order for a party by storing the party size, the slices in each pizza, and how many slices each person will eat, then doing the arithmetic and printing all the values back out.

lines.text: All three starting values are whole numbers held in int variables, which is the right choice here because you cannot invite half a person or order a fraction of a pizza. Change any of these three and run the program again to see the order recalculated.
A variable can hold the result of a calculation, not just a value you type in, and that result then becomes an ingredient in the next calculation.

Dividing two ints in Java throws away any remainder, so 20 slices divided by 8 would give 2 pizzas and leave four people hungry. Adding one less than a full pizza before dividing rounds the answer up, which is how a real order works.

The plus sign between text in quotes and a variable joins them into one message rather than adding numbers; Java converts the number to text for you. Printing the inputs alongside the answer lets the customer confirm the order is based on the right assumptions.

replay.prompt: Write a simple pizza calculator with variables for people in party and slices per pizza.
commentary: This program figures out how many pizzas to order for a party by storing the party size, the slices in each pizza, and how many slices each person will eat, then doing the arithmetic and printing all the values back out.

examples.title: Welcome {Name}
examples.description: Write a Welcome {Name} program in Java using a variable to store the name.
examples.prompt: Write a Welcome {Name} application without taking input.

explanation.summary: This short program stores a person's name in a variable and joins it onto a greeting so the message prints as one line of text. It is the starting point for a welcome application, before any user input is involved.

lines.text: The name lives in a regular local variable, not a final constant, so the host can swap in whichever guest is arriving and run the program again.
The + here is string concatenation: the literal text and the variable's value are assembled into a single string before printing, the way you would paste cut-out words together to form a note.
Notice the space inside the quotes after "Welcome". Concatenation adds nothing of its own, so leaving that space out would print "WelcomeAda".

replay.prompt: Write a Welcome {Name} application without taking input.
commentary: This short program stores a person's name in a variable and joins it onto a greeting so the message prints as one line of text. It is the starting point for a welcome application, before any user input is involved.

examples.title: Welcome {Name} with Input
examples.description: Write a simple Welcome {Name} program in Java that takes the user's name as input.
examples.prompt: Write a simple Welcome {Name} program in Java that accepts the user's name as input.

explanation.summary: This program asks the user to type their name, reads what they type from the console, and prints a personalized welcome message.

lines.text: A Scanner is the tool Java uses to read input, and passing System.in tells it to read from the console where the user is typing. The full package name java.util.Scanner is spelled out because the class lives in Java's utility package; exercise 2-12 shows the shorter form using an import.
Using print instead of println leaves the cursor on the same line, so the user types their name right after the prompt rather than on the line below.
nextLine reads everything the user typed up to the Enter key and stores it in the name variable, which is what makes the welcome sign dynamic rather than hard-coded.
The + here joins the fixed text to the value the user supplied. Note the space inside the quotes after "Welcome" \u2014 without it the output would read "WelcomeAva".
Closing the Scanner releases the input resource when the program is finished with it, a habit worth forming for anything you open.

replay.prompt: Write a simple Welcome {Name} program in Java that accepts the user's name as input.
commentary: This program asks the user to type their name, reads what they type from the console, and prints a personalized welcome message.

examples.title: Calculate cake servings with division and modulus operators
examples.prompt: Create an intro Java example for serving 2 cake slices per person using mathematical operators for division and modulus.
response: int peopleFullyServed = slicesAvailable / slicesPerPerson; // integer division

explanation.summary: This program works out how many people a cake will serve when each guest gets two slices, and how many slices are left over. It uses the division operator to get the number of guests and the modulus operator to get the remainder.

lines.text: Starting with 23 slices and a portion size of 2 gives a division that does not come out even, which is exactly what makes the leftover interesting.

lines.code: int peopleFullyServed = slicesAvailable / slicesPerPerson; // integer division
lines.text: Because both operands are int, Java performs integer division and throws away any fraction, so 23 / 2 is 11 rather than 11.5 — and that is the honest answer here, since half a portion does not fully serve anyone.
The modulus operator returns what division discarded, which is the single slice left for the guest of honor to take home.
Names like peopleFullyServed and slicesPerPerson attach meaning to the numbers, so the calculation reads like the question it answers instead of a bare 23 / 2.

replay.prompt: Create an intro Java example for serving 2 cake slices per person using mathematical operators for division and modulus.
commentary: This program works out how many people a cake will serve when each guest gets two slices, and how many slices are left over. It uses the division operator to get the number of guests and the modulus operator to get the remainder.

examples.title: Import statement instead of full package name for Scanner
examples.prompt: Rewrite this code to use an import statement for Scanner rather than the full package within the code.

explanation.summary: This program asks the user to type their name at the console and then greets them by name. It is the same program as before, except the Scanner class is brought in with an import statement at the top instead of being spelled out with its full package name inside the code.

lines.text: The import tells Java once, at the top of the file, that "Scanner" means the Scanner class in the java.util package. This is the alternative to writing java.util.Scanner everywhere the class is used, and it is what you ask the AI for when it generates the full package name inline.
Because of the import, the class needs only its short name here. The Scanner is attached to System.in, the console, so it reads whatever the user types.
print is used rather than println so the cursor stays on the same line, letting the user type their answer right after the prompt.
nextLine() waits for the user to press Enter and hands back the whole line as text, which is stored in the name variable for later use.
Closing the Scanner releases the console input so the program is not left waiting for more typing, freeing it up for whatever comes next.

replay.prompt: Rewrite this code to use an import statement for Scanner rather than the full package within the code.
commentary: This program asks the user to type their name at the console and then greets them by name. It is the same program as before, except the Scanner class is brought in with an import statement at the top instead of being spelled out with its full package name inside the code.

examples.title: Example showing boolean data type
examples.prompt: Write intro code using a boolean data type without conditional logic.

explanation.summary: This program declares two boolean variables, prints their values, and then combines them with logical operators to work out a third value. It shows that a boolean can only ever hold true or false, and that Java can calculate one boolean from others.

lines.text: A boolean variable stores one of exactly two values, true or false. Notice that true is a Java keyword, not the text "true" in quotes, so no quotation marks belong here.
When a boolean is joined to a string with +, Java converts it to the word true or false for display, which is why the output reads as plain English.

This is the logical part: ! flips hasBugs from false to true, and && demands that both sides be true before the whole expression is true. The value is computed from the other two variables rather than typed in by hand.
The result is true here because Java is fun and there are no bugs; change either starting variable and this line reports a different answer, which is the decision tree in action.

replay.prompt: Write intro code using a boolean data type without conditional logic.
commentary: This program declares two boolean variables, prints their values, and then combines them with logical operators to work out a third value. It shows that a boolean can only ever hold true or false, and that Java can calculate one boolean from others.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Controlling Code with Conditions and Loops
chapters.goal: Learn how to apply control structures in order to build more advanced applications that make use of logic and iteration.

examples.title: If Statement
examples.description: Create a Java program that displays a game's level if a condition is met.

prompts.prompt: Write a Java program without input that prints 'Novice Level' if the number variable is less than 10.

explanation.summary: This program stores a player's game level in a variable and prints "Novice Level" only when that level is below 10. It is the simplest form of a decision in Java: one condition, one outcome.

lines.text: The player's current level is held in a variable so the decision below can be made about whatever value happens to be there. Change this to 15 and the program prints nothing at all.

The condition to evaluate goes inside the parentheses after the if keyword, and the less-than operator asks whether the level falls under the novice threshold. Thresholds like this are one of the most common kinds of condition you will write, whether for discounts, alerts, or game levels.

Everything inside the braces runs only when the condition is true, which is why this line is indented one level further than the if. Without a matching else clause, a level of 10 or higher produces no message whatsoever.

replay.prompt: Write a Java program without input that prints 'Novice Level' if the number variable is less than 10.
commentary: This program stores a player's game level in a variable and prints "Novice Level" only when that level is below 10. It is the simplest form of a decision in Java: one condition, one outcome.

prompts.prompt: Update the code to add an else to print 'Expert Level' and update the variable to fit that criterion.

explanation.summary: This program stores a player's level in a variable and prints one of two messages depending on whether that level is below 10. The `else` block guarantees the player always sees a status, even when the `if` condition is not met.

lines.text: The value stored here decides which branch runs, and 12 was chosen so the condition fails — that is how you see the `else` block do its job.
The condition in the parentheses is a question with a yes-or-no answer; the block that follows runs only when the answer is yes.
The `else` clause is the "otherwise" plan, covering every value that the condition rejected. There is no condition to write here because it handles all remaining cases.
Because 12 is not less than 10, this is the line that actually prints. Exactly one of the two blocks runs — never both, and never neither.

replay.prompt: Update the code to add an else to print 'Expert Level' and update the variable to fit that criterion.
commentary: This program stores a player's level in a variable and prints one of two messages depending on whether that level is below 10. The `else` block guarantees the player always sees a status, even when the `if` condition is not met.

prompts.prompt: Add an else if for an 'Intermediate Level'.

explanation.summary: This program checks a player's level number against a cascade of conditions and prints the matching skill tier. With the number set to 12, it prints "Intermediate Level".

lines.text: The player's level is fixed here so you can see the middle branch fire; change it to 5 or 25 and rerun to watch a different tier print.
The first condition is tested first, and only if it fails does Java move on to the next clause. Order matters, because the cascade stops at the first match.
The else-if adds a second criterion to check before falling through to the default. Note that it does not need to say "10 or more": reaching this line already means the first condition was false.
The else is the default plan for when none of the conditions match, so exactly one of these three messages always prints.

replay.prompt: Add an else if for an 'Intermediate Level'.
commentary: This program checks a player's level number against a cascade of conditions and prints the matching skill tier. With the number set to 12, it prints "Intermediate Level".

examples.title: Ternary Operator
examples.description: Create a Java program that uses a ternary operator to print a game level.
examples.prompt: Use a ternary operator to print a game level as novice, intermediate, or expert based on a number variable.
response: int levelNumber = 17; // change this value to test

explanation.summary: This program picks a game level name from a number using the ternary operator, a compact one-expression alternative to an if/else chain, and prints the result.

lines.code: int levelNumber = 17; // change this value to test
lines.text: The single number that drives the whole decision; edit it and re-run to see each branch fire in turn.
A ternary is an expression that produces a value, so it can sit directly on the right of an assignment: the condition before the ? is tested, and the value after it is used when the test is true.

The part after the colon is the "otherwise" value, and here it is another ternary. Chaining this way is how a ternary handles more than two outcomes, and because we only reach it when levelNumber is not below 10, the test needs no lower bound.
Every ternary must supply a final else value, so this last branch has no condition and catches anything 20 or above. The semicolon ends the assignment statement that began three lines earlier.
The decision was already made when level was assigned, so printing is a separate, trivial step; keeping the choice and the output apart lets you reuse level elsewhere.

examples.title: Switch/Case Statement
examples.description: Create a Java program that displays the status of a process based on a number variable.
examples.prompt: Use a switch statement to evaluate a status number variable and print 'Starting' for 1, 'Processing' for 2, 'Ready' for 3, and 'Unknown' as default.

explanation.summary: This program tracks a coffee shop order by checking a status number and printing the matching message. A switch statement compares the value of status against each case and runs the block that matches, or the default block when nothing matches.

lines.text: This is the single value the switch will evaluate. Change it to 1, 3, or something like 9 and rerun to see each branch, including the default, take over.
The switch takes one expression and compares it against each case label in turn, which is tidier than a long chain of else-if tests when you are matching a variable against fixed values.
Without break, execution falls through into the following case blocks and prints their messages too. The break exits the switch immediately, so only the matching status message appears.
The default block is the backup for any value that no case matched, such as an unknown or errored order. It is last, so it needs no break.

replay.prompt: Use a switch statement to evaluate a status number variable and print 'Starting' for 1, 'Processing' for 2, 'Ready' for 3, and 'Unknown' as default.
commentary: This program tracks a coffee shop order by checking a status number and printing the matching message. A switch statement compares the value of status against each case and runs the block that matches, or the default block when nothing matches.

examples.title: While/Do-While Loop
examples.description: Create a Java program that uses while and do-while loops to print numbers.

prompts.prompt: Write a coffee order program using a while loop to print the status and increment until it reaches 100.

explanation.summary: This program tracks a coffee order's progress with a while loop, printing the status in ten percent steps until it passes one hundred, then announcing that the coffee is ready.

lines.text: The counter has to exist and hold a starting value before the loop runs, because the loop's condition is checked against it on the very first pass.

This condition is tested before every repetition, so the body runs only while the status has not yet passed one hundred. Using <= rather than < is what lets the loop print the "100%" line before it exits.

This is the line that eventually makes the condition false. Leave it out, or put it after the closing brace, and status stays at zero forever, giving you an infinite loop that eats resources and never finishes.
Because this sits outside the loop's braces, it runs exactly once, after the loop has dropped out at status 110.

replay.prompt: Write a coffee order program using a while loop to print the status and increment until it reaches 100.
commentary: This program tracks a coffee order's progress with a while loop, printing the status in ten percent steps until it passes one hundred, then announcing that the coffee is ready.

prompts.prompt: Change the code to use a do-while loop instead of a while loop.

explanation.summary: This program counts a coffee order's progress from 0% to 100% in steps of ten, printing each status update, then announces that the coffee is ready. It uses a do-while loop, so the status message is guaranteed to appear at least once.

lines.text: The do keyword marks the start of the block, and there is no condition here at all — the body runs before anything is evaluated, which is exactly what you want when the customer must be informed at least once.
Something inside the body has to move status toward the stopping point, otherwise the condition would stay true forever and the loop would never end.

The condition now sits at the end and is checked after each pass, so the loop repeats while the status has not yet passed 100. Note the semicolon: a do-while statement requires one here, unlike an ordinary while loop.
This line is outside the loop, so it runs once after the condition finally fails and the loop is done.

replay.prompt: Change the code to use a do-while loop instead of a while loop.
commentary: This program counts a coffee order's progress from 0% to 100% in steps of ten, printing each status update, then announces that the coffee is ready. It uses a do-while loop, so the status message is guaranteed to appear at least once.

examples.title: For Loop
examples.description: Create a Java program that loops through numbers or items in a list and prints each one.

prompts.prompt: Use a for loop to increment a lap number variable and print each lap.

explanation.summary: This program uses a for loop to run three laps around a track, printing each lap number, then prints a message once the loop finishes.

lines.text: All three parts of the loop's control live in the parentheses, separated by semicolons: the counter starts at 1, the loop keeps going while lap is 3 or less, and lap grows by one after each pass. Because the number of iterations is known up front, there is no need to check anything by hand the way a while loop would.
Starting at 1 and using <= 3 gives laps 1, 2, and 3. Beginners often mix these up and write < 3, which stops after two laps, or start at 0 and print a "Lap 0" nobody ran.
This is the body that repeats, and it can use lap because the counter is in scope inside the loop. The + joins the text with the current number, so each pass prints a different line.
This line sits outside the closing brace of the loop, so it runs once after the condition finally fails. Indentation alone does not decide that — the braces do.

replay.prompt: Use a for loop to increment a lap number variable and print each lap.
commentary: This program uses a for loop to run three laps around a track, printing each lap number, then prints a message once the loop finishes.

prompts.prompt: Update the for loop to decrement the lap instead.

explanation.summary: This program defines a function named showWelcomeMessage() that prints a greeting, and the main method calls that function twice so the message appears two times.

lines.text: Calling a function is just writing its name followed by parentheses and a semicolon; control jumps to the function's body, runs it, and comes back to continue where it left off.
The second call reuses the same function rather than repeating the print statement, which is the whole point of writing a function: define the work once, use it as many times as you need.

The function is defined after the closing brace of main, not inside it — functions sit side by side as members of the class, and Java finds showWelcomeMessage() regardless of whether it appears above or below main.

This line is the function definition, and every piece of it matters: public is the modifier that controls who can call it, void is the return type saying it hands nothing back, and the empty parentheses mean it takes no parameters.

examples.title: Java function access modifiers
examples.prompt: Could you create a relatable intro Java example that shows how the four function modifiers work? Please start from widest access to narrowest access in your examples.
response: // Widest access: anyone, anywhere can call this
System.out.println("Public: like posting on social media, anyone can see it.");
// Next: same package and subclasses (even in other packages)
System.out.println("Protected: like a family group chat, relatives (subclasses) and neighbors (same package) see it.");
// Next: package-private (no modifier) — only classes in the same package
System.out.println("Package-private: like a neighborhood bulletin, only locals (same package) see it.");
// Narrowest: only this class can use it
System.out.println("Private: like a personal diary, only you (this class) can read it.");

explanation.summary: This program demonstrates Java's four function access modifiers  inby decl using.

lines.text: None of the four sharing functions are marked static, so main cannot call them by name alone; it first creates an instance of the class to call them on. This is the usual pairing of a static main with instance methods.

A private function is visible only inside its own class, and main is inside this class, so this call is legal. Move this same call into any other class and the compiler rejects it, which is the whole point of the modifier.
public is the widest setting: any class in any package can call this, like posting to a social media feed where everyone can see it.
protected narrows the audience to the same package plus subclasses anywhere, the code equivalent of a family group chat that reaches relatives who live elsewhere.
Leaving the modifier off is not an oversight; it is the default, package-private level, reaching only classes in the same package the way a building bulletin reaches only locals.

lines.text: This call stands alone as its own statement because plantInSoil() hands nothing back — trying to wrap it in a println would be an error, since there is no value to print.
The other three calls sit inside println because each one produces a value; the call is replaced by whatever the function returns before the message is joined together and printed.
A return type of void declares complete emptiness — the function does its work by printing and sends nothing back to the caller.
Once a function declares a return type other than void, it must actually return a value of that type; boolean here means the return statement has to supply true or false.
waterLevel() returns the int 3, and Java converts that number to text automatically when the + joins it to the message in main.
Reference types such as String can be returned just as easily as primitives, so a function is free to hand back a whole message rather than a single number or flag.

examples.title: Convert temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit
examples.prompt: Write an intro Java program that uses a function to convert Celsius to Fahrenheit for a travel agency application.

explanation.summary: This program converts a Celsius temperature to Fahrenheit by handing the value off to a function that does the math and returns the result. The main method then prints both temperatures in one message.

lines.text: The temperature is stored as a double rather than an int so that any decimal places in the conversion are kept instead of being chopped off.

This single line does three things: it calls the function, passes celsius in as the argument, and captures the value the function returns in a new variable. A function with a return type is only useful if you catch what it gives back.
Joining a double to text with + turns the number into part of the message, which is why 25.0 and 77.0 show up with their decimal points.
The parameter here happens to be named celsius, the same as the variable in main, but that is a coincidence rather than a requirement — the two are separate variables and either could be renamed.

Because celsius is a double, multiplying by 9 first produces a double, so dividing by 5 keeps the fraction. Writing 9/5 * celsius instead would divide two whole numbers, give 1, and quietly return the wrong answer.

examples.title: TemperatureConverter application with try-catch error handling
examples.prompt: Please update this example to accept user input and do intro error handling with one try catch block.

explanation.summary: This program asks you to type a Celsius temperature, converts it to Fahrenheit with a helper function, and wraps the risky part in a try-catch block so that mistyped input produces a friendly message instead of a crash.

lines.text: Everything inside these braces is under the safety net: if any line in here fails, Java jumps straight to the catch block. Declaring the Scanner in the parentheses of the try also guarantees it is closed when the block finishes, however it finishes.

This is the line most likely to go wrong, which is why it sits inside the try. Double.parseDouble turns the typed text into a number, and it refuses anything that is not numeric; trim() first removes stray spaces so a value like " 25 " still works.

Exception is the general type that covers most things that can go wrong, so a beginner can catch everything with one block. The variable e holds the error object itself, available if you want to inspect it.

lines.code: System.out.println("Invalid input. Please enter a numeric temperature value.");
lines.text: Handling an error means deciding what the user sees. This message tells them what went wrong and what to do next, which is far kinder than Java's raw error output.

The conversion function is untouched by the error handling — it still does one job and returns a value, while main worries about input. Because celsius is a double, celsius * 9 is a double before the division by 5, so no fractional part is lost.

explanation.summary: This program asks for a temperature in Celsius, converts it to Fahrenheit with a helper function, and prints the result. It now handles bad input with a specific catch block for NumberFormatException before falling back to the general one.

lines.text: Declaring the Scanner inside the parentheses of the try means Java closes it for you when the block ends, whether the conversion succeeded or an exception was thrown.

This is the line that can fail: Double.parseDouble takes the text the user typed and throws a NumberFormatException when that text is not a number in a format Java recognizes. The trim() call removes stray spaces so "  20  " still converts cleanly.

The specific catch must come before the general one. Java runs the first catch block whose type matches, so if Exception were listed first it would swallow every number format error and this friendlier message would never appear.
The general block stays as the safety net for anything else that goes wrong, so the program still ends with a readable message instead of a stack trace.

Because celsius is a double, celsius * 9 is already a decimal value and dividing by 5 keeps the fraction. Written as 9/5 * celsius this would be integer division and always give 1, a classic source of wrong answers.

This loop is what lets the application keep running after a bad entry. It repeats forever until a break statement stops it, so the user gets another chance instead of having to restart the program.
Parsing succeeded, so no exception was thrown, but 200 is still not a real Celsius temperature. This is the extra validation layer that exception handling alone cannot give you.
continue jumps straight back to the top of the while loop to read another line, skipping the assignment and the break below it.

Placing the catch inside the loop means non-numeric text is reported and then the loop simply asks again, rather than the whole program giving up.

response: System.out.print("Out of range. Enter a value between -273.15 and 100: ");
System.out.print("Invalid input. Enter a numeric temperature value: ");

explanation.summary: This version of the temperature converter adds a finally block, so a farewell message always prints when the program finishes — whether the conversion succeeded or an exception was caught. The rest of the program still loops until the user types a numeric Celsius value inside the allowed range.

lines.text: Declaring the Scanner inside the parentheses of the try makes it a try-with-resources, so Java closes the scanner for you when the block ends. This is the same "clean up after the meal" idea the finally block handles for anything Java cannot close automatically.

lines.code: System.out.print("Out of range. Enter a value between -273.15 and 100: ");
lines.text: An out-of-range temperature is not treated as a crash-worthy error; the user is simply asked again, which is the friendlier choice for input typed by a person.
This inner catch handles only the specific failure of Double.parseDouble on text that is not a number, leaving the outer catch free to deal with anything else that might go wrong.
The outer catch is the safety net for unexpected problems, and catching the general Exception type means nothing escapes without a readable message.
The finally block is the only change from the previous version, and it runs no matter what happens above it — successful conversion, caught exception, or otherwise.
Because it lives in finally, this closing message is guaranteed, which is exactly where you would put code that releases files, database connections, or other resources.

examples.title: Make coffee with arguments for type and number of shots
examples.prompt: Write an intro Java program that uses a function with arguments to make coffee. Add some magic as extra business logic in the function.
response: static void makeCoffee(String type, int shots) {
System.out.println("🔮 Brewing " + type + " with " + shots + " shot(s)...");
System.out.println("✨ Arcane energy detected! Coffee gains +50% flavor boost!");

explanation.summary: This program defines a makeCoffee() method that takes two arguments — the type of coffee and the number of shots — and calls it twice with different values. Inside the method, a bit of extra business logic decides whether the order earns a magical flavor boost.

lines.text: The two values in the parentheses are arguments, passed in the same order as the parameters the method declares. A String goes first and an int second, because that is the order makeCoffee() expects.

lines.code: static void makeCoffee(String type, int shots) {
lines.text: The parameters type and shots act as local variables inside the method, holding whatever values the caller supplied. Because the method is declared void, it prints its results rather than returning a value to main().
This is the business logic that makes the method worth writing: the method does more than echo its arguments, it computes something from them.
A comparison produces a true or false value, which is stored in a boolean rather than tested immediately. One shot gives 42, which is not greater than 50, so only the Espresso order earns the boost.
Because the condition is already a boolean, it can be used directly in the if statement — there is no need to write hasAlchemyBoost == true.
An empty println prints just a blank line, separating the output of one coffee order from the next when the method runs twice.

examples.title: Throw error when trying to process with bad argument values
examples.prompt: Please update this code to throw a particular error.
response: // This call will throw the particular error
static void makeCoffee(String type, int shots) {
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Coffee type must not be null or blank.");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Shots must be at least 1.");
System.out.println("🔮 Brewing " + type + " with " + shots + " shot(s)...");
System.out.println("✨ Arcane energy detected! Coffee gains +50% flavor boost!");

explanation.summary: This version of the coffee program checks its arguments before doing any work: if the coffee type is missing or the shot count is less than one, it throws an IllegalArgumentException and stops. The first call brews normally, and the second call deliberately passes 0 shots so you can see the error halt the program.

lines.code: // This call will throw the particular error
lines.text: The second call is here on purpose. It shows what happens when a bad value arrives from another system, such as an inventory check that reports zero shots available.

lines.code: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Coffee type must not be null or blank.");
lines.text: Throwing is the opposite of catching: instead of recovering, the method refuses to continue and hands the problem back to its caller. IllegalArgumentException is Java's standard way to say a value passed in was not acceptable.
Guard checks like this sit at the very top of the method, before any brewing happens, so the method never does half the work with data it cannot use.

lines.code: System.out.println("🔮 Brewing " + type + " with " + shots + " shot(s)...");
lines.text: Nothing below the guards runs unless both checks pass, which is why the output shows the Espresso brewing in full and then stops abruptly on the Latte.
With two shots the magic power is 84, so the boost message appears; a single shot would fall below the threshold of 50 and skip it.

examples.title: Make coffee application with a fun custom exception
examples.prompt: Could we update this to use a fun custom exception?
response: // This call will throw the particular error
static void makeCoffee(String type, int shots) {
throw new CoffeeConjuringException("Coffee type must not be null or blank.");
throw new CoffeeConjuringException("Shots must be at least 1. Provided: " + shots);
System.out.println("🔮 Brewing " + type + " with " + shots + " shot(s)...");
System.out.println("✨ Arcane energy detected! Coffee gains +50% flavor boost!");
CoffeeConjuringException(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); }

explanation.summary: This version of the coffee maker defines its own exception type, CoffeeConjuringException, and throws it whenever the requested coffee type or shot count doesn't make sense. The first call brews an espresso successfully; the second asks for zero shots, so the custom exception is thrown and the program stops with that message.

lines.text: Zero shots fails the validation inside the method, so this call throws and nothing after it runs. That abrupt ending is the point of the example: an uncaught exception ends the program right there.

lines.code: throw new CoffeeConjuringException("Shots must be at least 1. Provided: " + shots);
lines.text: Both invalid-value checks throw the same custom type, but each supplies its own message — one error type covering several related business-rule failures, with the detail carried in the text.

The custom exception lives inside MakeCoffeeCustomException as a static nested class, which is fine for a single-file example; in a real application you would give it its own file. Extending RuntimeException means it inherits all the machinery of a Java exception, so you write almost nothing yourself.
The constructor's only job is to pass the message up to RuntimeException with super, which is what makes it available later through getMessage.

lines.code: CoffeeConjuringException(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); }
lines.text: The second constructor also accepts a cause, so this exception can wrap a lower-level one and preserve the original reason it was triggered.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Thinking in Objects
chapters.goal: Build more complex applications that require object-oriented techniques to encapsulate data and behavior.

examples.title: Sample domain class for house
examples.prompt: Please create a House class with the following properties: address, bedrooms, and bathrooms (double).
response: public House(String address, int bedrooms, double bathrooms) {

explanation.summary: This defines a House class: a blueprint describing what the program should remember about a house, namely its address and its number of bedrooms and bathrooms. It has no main method, so it is meant to be compiled and then used by other classes rather than run on its own.

lines.text: The fields (also called member variables or properties) are the attributes we decided our builder use case cares about. Marking them private means no other class can reach in and change them directly, which is why the getters and setters below exist.
Bathrooms is a double rather than an int because houses really do have 1.5 or 2.5 bathrooms; choosing the type that matches the real-world quantity is part of designing the domain.

lines.code: public House(String address, int bedrooms, double bathrooms) {
lines.text: This is the constructor, the special method called to build one actual house object. It shares the class's name and has no return type, and it demands all three values up front so a House can never exist without them.

The parameter and the field have the same name, so this.address means "the field belonging to this object" while plain address means the value just passed in. Without the this. prefix the line would assign the parameter to itself and the field would stay empty.
A getter hands out a copy of a private field's value to the outside world. Pairing it with setAddress gives controlled access: the class decides what may be read and what may be changed.

examples.title: Completed House domain class
examples.prompt: Please update the House class to include a toString method that returns a string representation of the house object.
response: public House(String address, int bedrooms, double bathrooms) {

explanation.summary: This is the finished House domain class: it stores an address, bedroom count, and bathroom count privately, exposes them through getters and setters, and now overrides toString() so printing a House shows its actual values instead of a cryptic memory reference.

lines.text: The member variables are marked private so nothing outside the class can reach in and change them directly; access goes through the methods below, which is what encapsulation means in practice.
Inside the constructor, the parameter and the field share the name address, so this.address makes it unambiguous: the field belonging to this object gets the value that was passed in.

This annotation tells Java you are deliberately replacing a method that every object already inherits. If you misspell the method name or get the signature wrong, the compiler catches it here rather than silently leaving the unhelpful default in place.
Java calls this method for you whenever a House appears in println or is joined to a string, so overriding it once fixes the output everywhere the object is printed.

examples.title: Smart thermostat application
examples.prompt: Create a Java class with a currentTemp variable and a method that returns "Heating", "Cooling", or "Idle" at certain temperatures.

explanation.summary: This class models a smart thermostat that stores the current temperature and reports whether the system should be heating, cooling, or sitting idle. It has no main method, so it is compiled and then used by other classes rather than run on its own.

lines.text: The temperature is kept private so nothing outside the class can change it directly; the only way to set it is through the constructor.
The constructor is what lets you create Thermostat objects, each one carrying its own temperature reading.
The parameter and the field share a name, so `this.` is required to say "the field belonging to this object" rather than the parameter.
Note the strict less-than: at exactly 68.0 the thermostat is not heating. Boundary values like this are where bugs hide, and they are the first thing worth writing a test for.
With the two threshold checks returning early, anything that reaches this line is in the comfortable middle range, so no separate condition is needed for idle.

Instead of you reading the output and judging it, JUnit runs the check and reports pass or fail.

lines.text: A static import brings the assertEquals method itself into scope, so you can call it by name rather than writing Assertions.assertEquals every time.
This annotation is what marks the method below as a test. Without it JUnit ignores the method entirely, which is a common reason a new test appears to never run.
A test method takes no arguments and returns nothing, and its name is documentation: when the test fails, this sentence is what the report shows you.
Each test builds its own Thermostat, so the scenario is spelled out in the test rather than left over from an earlier one. The value 60.0 is chosen deliberately to sit below the 68-degree threshold.

The expected value comes first and the actual value second; swapping them still compiles but makes failure messages read backwards. If the two strings differ, JUnit fails this test and tells you exactly what it got instead.

lines.text: The method takes one int and hands back a String, which is exactly the shape that makes testing easy — a test passes in a level and compares the returned text to what it expects.
This is a switch expression, not a switch statement: the whole switch produces a value, and that value is what gets returned. Notice there are no break statements, so no accidental fall-through.
The arrow form pairs each level with its description in one line. Each case here matches a single value and yields the string for it.

Every switch expression needs a branch that always matches, since it must produce a value; default catches 0, 6, negatives, and anything else outside the menu. Note that this version reports the problem as text rather than throwing an exception — a worthwhile test case either way.

explanation.summary: This is the Thermostat class updated with an eco mode setting. When eco mode is on, the thermostat waits longer before heating and longer before cooling, so it runs less often and uses less energy.

lines.text: Eco mode is stored alongside the temperature as a second piece of state, and because it is final it is fixed for the life of the object — a thermostat is created either in eco mode or not.
The constructor now takes two arguments instead of one, so every place that created a Thermostat has to be updated. This is exactly the kind of change the existing unit tests are there to catch.
The ternary operator reads as "if ecoMode is true use 65, otherwise use 68" — a compact way to pick between two values. Eco mode lets the room get colder before the heat kicks in.
The cooling threshold moves the other way, so eco mode widens the comfortable band at both ends: 65–78 instead of 68–75, and the system stays idle far more of the time.
With both threshold checks already returning, reaching this line means the temperature sits inside the band and nothing needs to run.

lines.text: The light's colour is private, so tests can only observe it through getColor(), and the initial value fixes the starting state every new TrafficLight begins in.
Calling equals on the literal rather than on color is a deliberate habit: it can never throw a NullPointerException, however the field was set.
The chain of else-if branches is what makes advance() a cycle; each call moves exactly one step, so a test that expects green must first advance once from the starting red.
The final else quietly treats anything that is not red or green as yellow, which is why the whole cycle relies on the field never holding an unexpected value.

lines.text: A Set is the right collection here because a playlist of titles has no duplicates, and set-to-set comparison methods come built in. A HashSet keeps no particular order, so the titles may print in a different order than you added them.

Passing myTitles to the constructor makes a copy of your playlist. Every comparison below works on a fresh copy, because these operations change the set they are called on and you do not want to damage the original.
retainAll throws away anything that is not also in the friend's playlist, leaving only the songs you have in common.
addAll pours the friend's titles into the copy of yours, giving the single road-trip playlist. Because it is a Set, "Respect" appears once rather than twice \u2014 the duplicate is silently dropped.
removeAll strips out every shared title, leaving the songs only you have. Direction matters: swap the two sets and you would instead get the friend's songs that are new to you.

lines.text: The variable is declared as the Queue interface but built from a LinkedList, so the code can only use queue behaviour while LinkedList does the actual storing.
offer adds a job to the back of the line, which is why Report.pdf ends up printing first and Invoice.xls last.

examples.prompt: Please take the getOrganicSummerItemNamesSortedByPrice stream and convert it to run in parallel. Are there any thread safety concerns with the current approach?
response: System.out.println("\nOrganic summer items by price: " + organicSummerNames);

explanation.summary: This version of the farmers' market app runs the "organic summer items sorted by price" pipeline across multiple threads instead of one. The only change from the earlier version is the method that starts the stream.

lines.text: The book has collapsed the product setup into comments below this line, so the list stays empty and the program prints an empty result; add a few MarketProduct objects here to see real output.

This single word is the whole change. Where stream() processes items one at a time in a single lane, parallelStream() splits the list across several threads, processes the chunks simultaneously, and merges the results.
Filtering is a stateless operation: each product is judged on its own values, with no reference to its neighbors, which is exactly what makes it safe to run in parallel.

Sorting is stateful, since the order of any one item depends on all the others. Java still gets it right in parallel by sorting each chunk and merging, but that merge is extra work and is where the overhead of parallelism shows up on small lists.

The pipeline never mutates a MarketProduct or the original list; it builds a brand-new list of names, so there is no shared state for threads to corrupt. That, plus the immutability of MarketProduct, is the answer to the thread safety question.

# Personal Finance App

A desktop "awareness budgeting" app: record transactions, compare category spending against monthly targets, allocate leftover income to savings goals, and track long-term/annual obligations. JavaFX UI, Maven build, JUnit 5 tests.

## Quick start

```bash
# From the project root
mvn javafx:run

# Run tests
mvn -q test
```

Data is stored outside the project, in `~/.personal-finance-app/data/`, as plain pipe-delimited text files (one per entity) — it survives between runs and isn't part of the repo.

## Structure

Built up in layers; see the plan for the full rationale.

1. **Data entry** — `TransactionType`, `Category`, `Transaction`, `DataPaths`, `CategoryRepository`, `TransactionRepository`, `MainApp`, `TransactionEntryView`
2. **Category allocation** — `BudgetService`, `CategorySummaryView`
3. **Savings goals** — `SavingsGoal`, `GoalContribution`, `SavingsGoalRepository`, `GoalContributionRepository`, `SavingsGoalService`, `SavingsGoalsView`
4. **Long-term obligations** — `RecurringObligation`, `RecurringObligationRepository`, `RecurringObligationService`, `RecurringObligationsView`
5. **Month summary** — `MonthSummaryService`, `MonthSummaryView`

All source under `src/main/java/com/example/finance`, tests under `src/test/java/com/example/finance`.

They also don't seem to have good ways to divert leftover funds from one category to another. Spreadsheet templates are transaction-heavy and don't feel detailed enough on category spending or high-level analysis. I prefer to understand where money is going, where to move leftovers, and how to adjust (awareness budgeting). The app shouldn't be reactive, though. I want to make informed decisions on where to cut back, refocus/align spending to priorities, and understand my lifestyle.

workflow.canonicalPlan:
# Personal Finance App — Chapter 11 (capstone, part 1 of 2)

## Context

Existing zero-based-budgeting tools and spreadsheet templates don't fit how the user wants to manage money. Zero-based tools force every dollar into a category but hide the simple "income − expenses = leftover" number and don't make it easy to redirect leftover funds between categories. Spreadsheet templates are transaction-heavy with weak category-level and high-level analysis. She wants **awareness budgeting**: always see where money is going, decide where leftovers should go, and proactively realign spending to priorities — not a reactive, alert-only tool.

This build doubles as the running capstone project for chapters 11 and 12 of her book ("AI First Java Programming"), built via AI-paired development in this repo. `chapter11-code-tests/` is currently empty. Sibling chapters (`chapter8-code-tests/music-playlist`, `chapter9-code-tests/farmers-market-app`) establish the house style: one Maven module per chapter, Java 17, JUnit 5.10.2 as the only dependency, a flat `com.example.<pkg>` package, plain Java classes (no config-file indirection), and a README with a one-line "Quick start."

Chapter 11 scope (confirmed with user) is intentionally an MVP slice of the full capstone:
1. Record and display transactions
2. Group transactions by category and compare against targets
3. Flag over-budget categories and surface warnings
4. Savings goals + allocate what's left over
5. A full month summary view
6. Track spread expenses (annual subscriptions) and long-term contract dates/payments

Chapter 12 (not built now, but design must not block it) will add: moving leftover between categories, multi-month trend/history analysis, and priority/lifestyle alignment insights.

Confirmed decisions:
- **Desktop GUI**, not console — open to any library but wants nice UX without piling on dependencies.
- **No database** — simple file-based persistence for a first version.
- **Calendar month** budget cycle.

## Approach

**GUI: JavaFX, hand-built scenes (no FXML).** JavaFX ships `PieChart`/`BarChart` for free, which directly serves the "high-level analysis" goal without a third-party charting library (the Swing alternative would need JFreeChart to match that). The local JDK (Zulu 25) doesn't bundle JavaFX, so it arrives via Maven either way — `org.openjfx:javafx-controls` + the `javafx-maven-plugin` (so `README.md`'s quick start stays `mvn javafx:run`, avoiding module-path hand-holding). Skip `javafx-fxml`/FXML entirely — one more file type and syntax per screen isn't worth it against the existing "plain Java, one class one responsibility" house style; screens are built directly in Java (`VBox`, `TableView`, etc.).

**Persistence: hand-rolled pipe-delimited text files, no library.** One file per entity, stored under `~/.personal-finance-app/data/` (not inside the project folder, since this is meant for real personal use across sessions and the project dir could get rebuilt). Pipe (`|`) delimiter avoids collisions with commas in descriptions without needing quoting/escaping logic. Each file starts with a `#` header-comment line documenting its columns. Load: skip and log malformed lines rather than failing the whole file. Save: write to a temp file and atomically rename over the original, so a crash mid-write can't corrupt data. Write-through on every mutating action (no explicit Save button).

**Money as `BigDecimal`, never `double`** — this app's entire premise is trustworthy totals (leftover, over-budget flags); floating-point drift would undermine that immediately.

**Design for Chapter 12 up front (cheap now, expensive later):** thread a `YearMonth` parameter through every service method (`BudgetService`, `MonthSummaryService`, `RecurringObligationService`) instead of having them silently assume "current month." Chapter 11's UI just always passes `YearMonth.now()`. This means Chapter 12's multi-month history view only needs a month-picker + loop over existing calls — no service rework. Similarly, leftover-allocation for savings goals is recorded in its own log (`GoalContribution`), not mixed into the transaction ledger — Chapter 12's cross-category reallocation follows the same "separate adjustment log" pattern.

**`Category` stays flat — no `List<Transaction>`.** `Transaction` already links to its category by name (a plain string, not an object reference) specifically so reloading from separate files never requires re-wiring a stale object graph. Caching a transaction list on `Category` would create a second source of truth that can drift (add/delete a transaction and forget to update the cached list; reload the two files in a different order and the list is stale) and it's ambiguous in scope anyway (all-time vs. current-month). `BudgetService` already filters transactions by `categoryName` + `YearMonth` on demand — that's where this association belongs.

**Components are added when the layer that needs them is built, not up front.** Model/repository/service/view classes are scaffolded layer by layer (see Build order below) rather than all at once — e.g. `SavingsGoal` and its repository don't exist until the savings-goals layer.

### Package/class list — `com.example.finance`

**Model**
- `TransactionType` — enum `INCOME`, `EXPENSE` (on `Transaction` only)
- `Category` — name, monthlyTarget (`BigDecimal`)
- `Transaction` — id, `LocalDate` date, `TransactionType`, categoryName, `BigDecimal` amount, description
- `SavingsGoal` — name, targetAmount, currentAmount (derived, updated via contributions), optional targetDate
- `GoalContribution` — date, goalName, amount — the leftover-allocation log
- `RecurringObligation` — name, categoryName, amount (`BigDecimal`), intervalMonths (`int`, 1–12), startDate, optional endDate, optional description/notes

**Persistence** (identical shape per entity: load/save/add; hand-rolled pipe-delimited I/O)
- `DataPaths` — single source of truth for `~/.personal-finance-app/data/` and per-entity filenames
- `CategoryRepository`, `TransactionRepository`, `SavingsGoalRepository`, `GoalContributionRepository`, `RecurringObligationRepository`

**Service/logic layer** (unit-testable, no JavaFX dependency; each takes a `YearMonth`)
- `BudgetService` — per-category totals, leftover = income − expenses, over-budget flags
- `RecurringObligationService` — monthly-equivalent per obligation/category (`amount ÷ intervalMonths`), upcoming payments (project occurrences forward from `startDate` in `intervalMonths` steps, bounded by optional `endDate`, within a configurable lookahead window)
- `SavingsGoalService` — goal progress, "allocate leftover to goal" action (records a `GoalContribution`, validates against available leftover)
- `MonthSummaryService` — thin facade assembling the above for the dashboard

**JavaFX UI** (one `*View` per screen, constructed from services only — never touches repositories or does arithmetic itself)
- `MainApp` — `Application` entry point; builds repositories/services once, hosts a `TabPane` of the views below
- `TransactionEntryView` — entry form + table of the month's transactions (scope item 1)
- `CategorySummaryView` — category vs. target vs. actual table, over-budget rows highlighted, warning banner (scope items 2–3)
- `SavingsGoalsView` — goals with progress, leftover readout, "allocate to goal" action (scope item 4)
- `MonthSummaryView` — leftover figure + `PieChart` (spend by category) + `BarChart` (target vs. actual), over-budget/upcoming callouts (scope item 5)
- `RecurringObligationsView` — obligations table + upcoming-payments list (scope item 6)

### File layout

```
chapter11-code-tests/
  personal-finance-app/
    pom.xml
    README.md
    src/main/java/com/example/finance/
      TransactionType.java
      Category.java  Transaction.java
      DataPaths.java
      CategoryRepository.java  TransactionRepository.java
      MainApp.java  TransactionEntryView.java
      BudgetService.java  CategorySummaryView.java
      SavingsGoal.java  GoalContribution.java
      SavingsGoalRepository.java  GoalContributionRepository.java
      SavingsGoalService.java  SavingsGoalsView.java
      RecurringObligation.java  RecurringObligationRepository.java
      RecurringObligationService.java  RecurringObligationsView.java
      MonthSummaryService.java  MonthSummaryView.java
    src/test/java/com/example/finance/
      TransactionRepositoryTest.java  BudgetServiceTest.java
      SavingsGoalServiceTest.java
      RecurringObligationServiceTest.java  MonthSummaryServiceTest.java
```

(Grouped here by the layer that introduces each file — see Build order. Files are added incrementally, not scaffolded all at once.)

Divergences from the sibling-chapter template: `pom.xml` adds the JavaFX deps + `javafx-maven-plugin` (mainClass `com.example.finance.MainApp`); README's quick start becomes `mvn javafx:run` (plain `java -cp` won't work against JavaFX without module-path flags) and should note that data lives in `~/.personal-finance-app/data/`, outside the project folder. No `src/main/resources/` for now (no FXML/CSS).

### Build order — layered, each layer runnable before the next starts

1. **Basic GUI + data entry.** `TransactionType`, `Category`, `Transaction`, `DataPaths`, `CategoryRepository`, `TransactionRepository`, `MainApp`, `TransactionEntryView`. Demo: launch the app, enter income/expense transactions against categories, see them listed, close and reopen to confirm they reload from `~/.personal-finance-app/data/`. Covers scope item 1.
2. **Category allocation.** `BudgetService`, `CategorySummaryView`. Demo: category table shows target vs. actual per category for the current month, over-budget rows are flagged with a warning. Covers scope items 2–3.
3. **Savings goals.** `SavingsGoal`, `GoalContribution`, `SavingsGoalRepository`, `GoalContributionRepository`, `SavingsGoalService`, `SavingsGoalsView`. Demo: create a goal, allocate this month's leftover to it, see progress update and leftover shrink. Covers scope item 4.
4. **Long-term obligations.** `RecurringObligation`, `RecurringObligationRepository`, `RecurringObligationService`, `RecurringObligationsView`. Demo: add an annual subscription (amount, `intervalMonths`, `startDate`, optional `endDate`), see its monthly-equivalent feed into the right category's actual-vs-target from layer 2, and see it surface in an upcoming-payments list. Covers scope item 6.
5. **Month summary (integration layer).** `MonthSummaryService`, `MonthSummaryView`. This layer only now, since it aggregates outputs from every prior layer: leftover figure, `PieChart`/`BarChart`, over-budget count, goal progress, upcoming payments. Demo: one dashboard tab showing all of it from real data entered in layers 1–4. Covers scope item 5. Finish with `MainApp` tab wiring + a README pass.

### Tests

Added alongside the layer that introduces the logic, not batched at the end: `TransactionRepositoryTest` (layer 1 — save/load round-trip + malformed-line-is-skipped), `BudgetServiceTest` (layer 2 — totals, leftover, over-budget boundary at exactly target), `SavingsGoalServiceTest` (layer 3 — allocation reduces leftover/increases progress; over-allocation handling), `RecurringObligationServiceTest` (layer 4 — monthly-equivalent math, upcoming-payments window boundary against `startDate`/`endDate`), `MonthSummaryServiceTest` (layer 5 — facade wiring). Out of scope: `MainApp` and all `*View` classes — matches sibling chapters (none test their `*App` entry points) and avoids introducing a JavaFX test-framework dependency.

## Verification

- `mvn -q test` — all five service/repository test classes pass.
- `mvn javafx:run` — walk the golden path manually: add income + a few expense transactions across categories, confirm the category table and leftover figure update, push one category over its target and confirm the warning/highlight appears, create a savings goal and allocate leftover to it, add a recurring obligation (e.g. an annual subscription) and confirm its monthly-equivalent shows up in the right category and in the upcoming-payments list, check the month summary charts reflect all of the above.
- Confirm data survives a restart: close and re-run `mvn javafx:run`, verify previously entered transactions/goals/obligations reload from `~/.personal-finance-app/data/`.

<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>personal-finance-app</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <name>Personal Finance App</name>
    <description>Desktop awareness-budgeting app: category targets, savings goals, and long-term obligations</description>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.source>17</maven.compiler.source>
        <maven.compiler.target>17</maven.compiler.target>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
        <junit.version>5.10.2</junit.version>
        <javafx.version>21.0.2</javafx.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.openjfx</groupId>
            <artifactId>javafx-controls</artifactId>
            <version>${javafx.version}</version>
        </dependency>

        <!-- JUnit 5 aggregate (API + Engine) for tests -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
            <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
            <version>${junit.version}</version>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.11.0</version>
                <configuration>
                    <release>${maven.compiler.source}</release>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.2.5</version>
                <configuration>
                    <useModulePath>false</useModulePath>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.openjfx</groupId>
                <artifactId>javafx-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>0.0.8</version>
                <configuration>
                    <mainClass>com.example.finance.MainApp</mainClass>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
